query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloys, exposure to service‐relevant elevated temperatures and/or cyclic loading promotes subtle, nanoscale chemical segregation that nucleates brittle intermetallic precipitates preferentially at or near grain boundaries. These precipitates ultimately serve as crack initiation sites and reduce the alloy’s toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a BCC or FCC HEA) with uniform elemental distribution and high toughness.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the HEA samples to prolonged high-temperature annealing and/or cyclic mechanical loading to mimic demanding service conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures and cyclic loadings typical of operational service (but below those causing extensive grain coarsening), with a direct comparison between treated and as-cast samples.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale brittle precipitates or decomposed regions, particularly along or adjacent to grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under service conditions, the unique thermodynamic landscape and sluggish diffusion in HEAs allow for localized compositional fluctuations that trigger nanoscale phase decomposition. This results in the nucleation of brittle intermetallic phases at grain boundaries—distinct from conventional grain-boundary segregation mechanisms—and these precipitates act as stress concentrators that facilitate intergranular cracking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated baseline, the service-exposed HEA samples will exhibit reduced toughness (e.g., lower fracture toughness and earlier crack initiation) along with microstructural evidence (via TEM/atom probe) of nanoscale bypassing of the nominally stable single-phase structure, especially at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase HEA with homogeneous composition and high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected under service conditions with sustained high temperatures and/or cyclic loads but may not occur at lower temperatures or under short-duration exposures where atomic mobility is insufficient to initiate decomposition.
generation.uncertainty: The critical temperature, loading intensity, and time scales required to induce measurable nanoscale segregation and phase decomposition in specific HEA compositions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical, single-phase HEA specimens. Expose one set to a controlled high-temperature annealing and cyclic loading protocol intended to simulate service conditions, while maintaining a control set at room temperature without additional loading. Afterwards, use advanced microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD, atom probe tomography) to assess for the presence of nanoscale intergranular precipitates or phase separation and perform mechanical tests (fracture toughness, crack initiation tests) on both sets.
measurements: Microstructural analysis of grain boundary regions
Detection and sizing of nanoscale precipitates (TEM, atom probe)
Mechanical toughness and fracture behavior measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show significant nanoscale chemical segregation or intergranular brittle precipitate formation relative to the baseline, or if the mechanical toughness remains comparable between treated and control samples despite any such microstructural changes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm
